newsitem.title: PHILIPPINES: Manila blames manufacturing for GNP growth dip.
newsitem.headline: Manila blames manufacturing for GNP growth dip.

text.p: A slowdown in manufacturing was behind a slightly lower than expected rise in economic growth in the first quarter of this year, Planning Secretary Cielito Habito told reporters on Thursday.
Gross national product in January to March rose 6.1 percent, compared to a revised 6.9 percent a year earlier and the government target of 6.4 percent.
"The reason for the slowdown was due to the manufacturing sector," he said.
Economists earlier polled by Reuters had expected a rise of 6.3 percent on average.

However, Habito said the figures showed the Philippines' economy continued at a comfortably heatlhy pace, contrary to negative market expectations and said the slowdown in manufacturing was temporary.
The stock market and the peso have both come under strong pressure in recent weeks, largely on fears that the Philippines would suffer the same fate as Thailand.
The first quarter growth was supported by strong domestic production, with GDP up 5.0 percent versus 5.1 per cent.
"Sustained net inflows of factor incomes from abroad, which amounted to about 11.5 billion pesos in real terms likewise contributed to output growth during the same period," he said.
On the supply side, growth was fuelled by services and agriculture while fixed investment rose at a faster pace of 12.3 percent in the quarter compared to a year ago.
One of the key factors behind the recent stock market tumble was fears of a property collapse.
Figures show the construction industry boomed during the quarter rising 16.4 percent from last year's 7.6 percent.
Investment in construction also surged, jumping 18 percent.
Disppointments were in trade, where exports only rose 7.4 percent in real terms due to drops in garments, crude coconut oil, and shellfish though in current dollar terms the rise was 17.4 percent.
Imports, by contrast rose a real 9.8 percent or 14.2 percent in current dollar terms.
Several industries put in a lacklustre performance, notably textiles, rubber products and metals.
Growth in the utilities sector was slow as as result of lower growth in other industries and mining and quarrying took a steep fall, dropping 19.4 percent.
Habito reitereated that growth for the rest of the year was likely to pick up and that the government's 7-8 percent target for the year was within reach.
